metadata.title: SponsorSQL: Plain-English Questions, Answers You Can Check
metadata.audience: INFO 7375 reviewers and Data Analyst hiring managers
metadata.persona: Atharva (first person; script written by Atharva Hambir with Claude; synthetic Kokoro voice, disclosed in the project's film/README.md)
metadata.note: INFO 7375 Final Project demo, four parts in order: executive summary (B00-B01), introduction (B02), methods (B03-B07), evaluation (B08-B11), outro (B12). Every number on screen comes from saved output of the real system in fall-2026/atharva-h/final-project (evidence/ and evals/results/), re-typeset for legibility and labelled as such. The SQL proposals were real Claude replies from separate Claude Code subagents on 2026-11-21, replayed by the agent; no live CLI call is shown or claimed. No Claude chat response is shown. The human gate prompt is shown as the interactive prompt text; no owner decision is claimed.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Atharva. This is my final project, Sponsor S Q L. International students like me want to know which employers file H one B paperwork for jobs like ours. That information is public, but it sits in one giant government spreadsheet that most students can't search.

beats.narration_text: So Sponsor S Q L does one simple thing. You ask in plain English. It gives you the number, the S Q L query behind it, and the rows it counted, so you can check the answer, instead of just trusting it blindly.

beats.narration_text: What already exists? Sites like My Visa Jobs and an H one B salary explorer let you search filings by employer and job title. A chatbot can write the query: when I asked Chat G P T about data analyst cases in Boston, it said forty, but nothing checked it. Sponsor S Q L adds two things: you see the query and the rows, and I publish how often it's wrong.

beats.narration_text: Now, how it works. The data is the Labor Department's latest file of Labor Condition Applications, the form an employer files before hiring someone on an H one B. The loader checks the file's fingerprint, drops five hundred ninety-five thousand blank rows, and keeps four hundred thirty-seven thousand real filings, with eighteen public columns. Contact names and emails are never loaded.

beats.narration_text: It's an agent, so it runs a loop. Observe the question. Decide whether to refuse it, then ask Claude for a query. Act: run it. Record every step. And stop: on a person's decision, a refusal, or a spent budget of two tries and ten seconds per query.

beats.narration_text: The tool is a database query, guarded by a permission policy: a short list, written in code, of what the tool is allowed to do. Here, that's only reading one table. The database opens read-only, so anything else, like changing or deleting data, is blocked before it runs. In this real output, a delete and a hidden second statement are refused, and the table still has every row.

beats.narration_text: What it needs: Python's standard library, SQLite, and my Claude Code account. No packages installed, no paid credits. The Claude command line wasn't logged in, so the queries tested here came from separate Claude sessions, saved word for word and replayed.

beats.narration_text: How do I know it works? I tested it on two sets of questions. The development set: ten questions I used while building, to find mistakes and fix them. The held-out set: five new questions kept aside until the very end, to check the fixes also work on questions it wasn't tuned for. For each question, separate code counted the right answer from the data. That's the answer key. Both sets were locked before testing, so nothing could change after seeing results. To pass: eight out of ten, four out of five, and no unsafe query.

beats.narration_text: First, the development set. The first try got four out of ten right. It matched job titles too loosely: Metadata Analyst counted as a Data Analyst, because it contains those words. So I added a rule to Claude's instructions to match whole words in job titles, and the score rose to nine out of ten. The one miss: a few job titles end in invisible characters, like tabs. The answer key removed them and the query didn't, so a few counts were off by one or two. Last, the held-out set, run only once: five out of five.

beats.narration_text: I also tried to break it on purpose. Ten deliberate failures, unsafe queries, a runaway query, questions about contact details or visa chances, and a stale approval, were all stopped as predicted. The original title bug, triggered on purpose, was caught by the answer key.

beats.narration_text: An independent reviewer found eighteen problems, and the ones code could fix were fixed. Three limits remain. The final version of Claude's instructions was tested before I reviewed it; I've reviewed it since. The answer keys share their rules with the system. And the replies were replayed, not live. So the honest claim is narrow: one public file, answers you can check. Ship, narrow, or defer is my sign-off, still open.
